A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same low-rank RBM pretraining and Parallel Trajectory Tempering (PTT) work. Their complete main texts, figures, tables, equations, and appendices support comparison despite substantial expansion and reorganization.

before.justification: v1 reports original training, generation, likelihood, sampling, and privacy results on MNIST01, Mickey, and human genome data.

after.justification: v2 reports original experiments on the retained and additional datasets, including exact-likelihood validation, sampler comparisons, sensitivity studies, and equilibration measurements.

M1.justification: v2 adds online Tr-AIS using persistent evaluation chains and per-update importance weights, and separates standalone offline Tr-AIS from PTT-based estimation (Section 5.1, Appendix D). It extends the existing bias treatment with a separate dataset-mean direction entering only the visible bias (Appendix A.3). The underlying RCM pretraining framework and PTT swap rule are retained.

E1.justification: v2 adds generative-model evaluation on 2D Ising configurations, 32-by-32 black-and-white CelebA images, and full MNIST, while retaining MNIST01, Mickey, and human genome data (Table 2, Figures 2 and 16). This materially broadens coverage to physical configurations, faces, and the remaining digit classes.

E2.justification: v2 directly evaluates Parallel Tempering, reference-distribution Parallel Tempering, and Stacked Tempering against PTT on retained datasets (Figure 4); v1 directly compared PTT with Gibbs sampling and discussed Stacked Tempering through published speedups. v2 also adds reference-distribution AIS comparisons. JarRBM disappears from the plotted training comparisons, although its implementation and failure discussion remain.

E3.justification: Table 3 changes HGD hidden units from 185 to 200 and Mickey from 100 to 200. v2 introduces small-RBM exact-enumeration validation and varying AIS schedules. Sampling comparisons count Gibbs steps across all replicas instead of v1's per-replica steps, and the main PTT acceptance target changes from approximately 0.30 to 0.25. Figure 10 additionally selects models at comparable privacy loss.

E4.justification: New Appendices B.1 and F examine equilibration, exchange-acceptance sensitivity, and learning-rate/hidden-width sensitivity using autocorrelation curves, cost curves, and likelihood grids. Appendix H adds longitudinal privacy and overfitting analyses beyond v1's endpoint comparison. Conversely, v1's supplementary sampling case studies for PCD- and JarRBM-trained machines are removed.

E5.justification: v1 reports jump-count averages over 100 chains without corresponding uncertainty reporting or a stated training-replication count. v2 Figure 2 newly reports 10 trainings and standard-deviation bands conditional on a common low-rank initialization. Figure 4 increases the sampling ensemble to 1000 chains and reports errors of the mean; Appendix B.1 also specifies uncertainty estimation for autocorrelation times.

E6.justification: v2 adds exact-likelihood error curves, broader training results, runtimes, sensitivity scores, and equilibration estimates, while removing JarRBM curves and v1's acceleration-factor table. For example, its new MNIST01 grid reports test likelihoods of -73.99 ± 2.71 for PCD and -66.37 ± 1.10 for pretraining plus PCD at 1000 hidden units and learning rate 0.01 (Figure 7). Results involving changed widths, estimators, or cost accounting are not same-setting gains over v1.

T1.justification: Appendix D adds AIS path-weight identities, and Appendix E derives forward/backward transition corrections before applying the symmetric-update assumption already stated in v1. Appendix G introduces substantial Curie-Weiss and phase-transition mathematics, while Appendix A.3 formalizes the additional bias direction. The new Appendix G nevertheless contains an internal inconsistency: its positive Hm term favors negative magnetization for positive H, contrary to the accompanying interpretation.

C1.justification: v2 makes inexpensive online likelihood evaluation an explicit central contribution, whereas v1 emphasized pretraining, PTT sampling, and PTT-based likelihood estimation. Its conclusion also qualifies pretraining's benefits for tightly clustered datasets and acknowledges limited benefits during long training, narrowing v1's broadly positive generative-quality claims.

C2.justification: v2 explains why pretraining offers limited benefits on less clustered data and why long training can again lose equilibrium, recommending combination with optimized MCMC methods (Section 6). It also connects train/test likelihood divergence with increasing privacy loss and analyzes exchange-acceptance versus computational-cost tradeoffs (Appendices H and B.1). These substantially extend v1's interpretations and applicability boundaries.

D1.justification: v2 supplies RCM dimensionalities, hidden-unit counts, and pretraining times (Table 5), total training times (Table 4), and implementation details for persistent online-AIS chains (Appendix D.2). The printed code/data pointer changes from nbereux/fast-RBM to anonymousrbm/iclr-2025. These are additional reproducibility disclosures; repository accessibility itself cannot be established from the PDFs.

R1.justification: v2 explicitly positions its approach as a practical extension of earlier RCM work, identifying bias and sampling developments needed for real datasets. It substantially expands AIS/PT, equilibration, phase-transition, and neural/biomedical references, including Neal, Hukushima and Nemoto, Sokal, and Bravi. Several quantum and AdS application references from v1 are removed.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, related work, and conclusion are extensively rewritten. Section 5 is reorganized around trajectory annealing with separate likelihood-estimation and sampling subsections, and the main-text privacy section moves into Appendix H within a substantially reorganized supplement. The title, citation style, and headers also change.

P2.justification: Figure 2 changes from three-method density maps to scatter plots, marginal histograms, and likelihood curves; Figure 4 expands the sampler comparison and changes its cost axis. v2 adds accuracy, sensitivity, and equilibration plots plus timing tables. Low-rank generation panels move from Figure 1 to Figure 15, while the existing PTT schematic is retained as Figure 5.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens validation through exact-likelihood checks on small RBMs, direct comparisons with stronger samplers that account for replica count, replicated trainings, and equilibration diagnostics. These address important weaknesses in v1's evidence, while the new applicability limits make the conclusions better qualified. Removing explicit JarRBM results and introducing the Appendix G sign inconsistency are drawbacks, but they are outweighed by the stronger validation of the central methods.
